text: bivorous mammals. Humans can become in- fected by contact with infected animals or infected or con- taminated animal products, or by inhalation of anthrax spores. Person-to-person transmission has not been report- ed. Although rare in western countries it remains a prob- lem in many areas, including Africa, Asia, some southern European countries, the Americas, and parts of Australia. Anthrax has also been used as a weapon for biological warfare. In humans anthrax presents most often in the cutaneous form. Gastrointestinal or inhalation anthrax can also occur and in these types the prognosis is poor without prompt treatment. In cutaneous anthrax symptoms may develop within hours, or up to 12 days, after contact and initially involves a painless, pruritic papule, which enlarges to an ulcer. Later (2 to 6 days) a vesicle with a black eschar de- velops. The incubation period for inhalation anthrax is usually about 10 days. Initial symptoms are non-specific and resemble a flu-like illness with fever, non-productive cough, dyspnoea, fatigue, headache, malaise, sweats, weakness, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This initial stage may last from a few hours to days and is followed in some patients by a short period of recovery while others progress directly to respiratory failure. Gastrointestinal anthrax has an incubation period of up to 1 week (usually 2 to 5 days) and initial symptoms are fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, gastric ulcers, haematemesis, and diarrhoea (usually bloody). Systemic disease progresses rapidly and hypotension, shock, and death may occur 2 to 5 days after initial symptoms. The treatment of naturally occurring anthrax has tradi- tionally been with benzylpenicillin with ciprofloxacin or doxycycline (or other tetracycline) as alternatives. Other drugs with in vitro activity are aminoglycosides, amoxicil- lin, chloramphenicol, clindamycin, imipenem, linezolid, the macrolides, meropenem, rifampicin, and vancomy- cin.1-3 There are currently no clinical trial data on the opti- mal treatment for anthrax and treatment recommendations and guidelines1-3 are based largely on the experience gained during the 1979 incident in Sverdlovsk (accidental release of biological warfare agents), the 2001 attack in the USA (deliberate release), isolated case reports of naturally occurring disease, and in vitro data. Because of the risks of engineered drug-resistant strains of B. anthracis, inducible beta-lactamases, and in vitro resistance to ofloxacin, guidelines1-3 for the treatment of anthrax (occurring after deliberate release) recommend the use of 2 or more anti- bacterials which should be started as soon as possible. Cor- ticosteroids may be given as adjunctive therapy.
